summary: Ehrman narrowly wins by showing that some historically received Bibles attribute textually disputed words to Jesus, while White strongly defends recoverable doctrine and message continuity.

pro.context: Ehrman closes by referring to manuscript Bibles historically available to churches, each containing copying mistakes, including some within reported words of Jesus.

con.context: White closes by separating differences among surviving copies from false quotation, grounding his denial in recoverable apostolic teaching and stable gospel content.

moves.words: Ehrman models successive copying as an error-amplifying chain: later scribes inherit earlier mistakes, add new ones, and sometimes make uncertain corrections without the autograph.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman turns an abstract transmission problem into a concrete copying sequence in which inherited errors, fresh slips, and speculative corrections accumulate without an autograph for comparison. Principal limitation: The linear illustration establishes a genuine route to corruption but does not itself represent the branching, comparison, and geographical dispersion that White later makes central; its deliberately sequential architecture therefore understates cross-copy correction, independent exemplars, and the diagnostic value of disagreements among geographically separated descendants. Live burden: Ehrman must connect this possible chain to particular consequential readings, while White must show why surviving diversity reliably exposes rather than merely preserves early alterations. Locked score: The move supplies an intelligible causal foundation for the affirmative case, although its simplified genealogy leaves the debate’s strongest preservation mechanism unanswered at this stage, 83/100.

moves.words: White argues raw variant totals rise with manuscript abundance, while numerous geographically and temporally distributed copies also provide stronger comparative evidence for reconstructing earlier readings.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White supplies the necessary denominator for Ehrman’s headline number, explaining that every additional manuscript creates further opportunities to record differences while simultaneously expanding the evidence available for comparison. Principal limitation: The arithmetic relationship alone does not establish that witnesses are sufficiently early or genealogically independent, nor does abundance automatically recover the correct wording at a particular disputed passage. Live burden: White must show how the enlarged witness base constrains concrete alternatives across transmission lines; Ehrman must distinguish evidentially significant uncertainty from the variant total mechanically generated by many copies. Locked score: The move decisively neutralizes raw-count rhetoric and identifies a genuine reconstructive advantage, although manuscript quantity requires genealogical and chronological analysis before it establishes recovery, 87/100.

moves.words: Ehrman presents the woman-taken-in-adultery narrative as a beloved, moving story absent from the oldest authorities and inserted into John by later scribal transmission.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman chooses a substantial, familiar passage whose disputed textual status makes the practical difference between historical Bibles and reconstructed editions immediately visible to ordinary readers. Principal limitation: He does not argue that this addition uniquely creates an essential Christian belief, and White can concede its nonoriginality while contesting its effect on the debate’s broader stakes; consequently, the example proves secondary narrative attribution more readily than corruption of Christianity’s proclamation about forgiveness, judgment, or Jesus’ identity. Live burden: Ehrman must explain why a nonoriginal episode attributed to Jesus satisfies the motion even when doctrine survives elsewhere; White must justify any narrower definition of misquotation. Locked score: The example powerfully establishes an extended textual addition involving Jesus, directly supporting the ordinary-language motion despite limited force against overall theological continuity, 89/100.

moves.words: White separates variants into untranslatable differences, nonviable readings, and meaningful viable alternatives, reserving serious textual analysis for the comparatively small final category.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White supplies the debate’s clearest analytical taxonomy, preventing spelling slips and unsupported late readings from being counted as though each threatened interpretation equally. Principal limitation: Categorization does not answer which meaningful viable readings concern Jesus or how much uncertainty within that final class the motion permits; moreover, the boundaries between interpretively consequential and merely translatable differences require argued judgments rather than automatic placement in self-explanatory compartments. Live burden: White must move from numerical rarity to a defensible account of quotation, whereas Ehrman must show that selected residual variants are both viable and materially significant. Locked score: The framework sharply improves evidential hygiene and concedes the right cases for examination, earning substantial credit even though the decisive dispute begins precisely where its filtering ends, 89/100.

moves.words: Ehrman argues that Mark originally ended with the frightened women’s silence and that scribes supplied twelve later verses containing appearances, commissioning, tongues, snakes, and poison.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The longer ending gives Ehrman another extensive, readily testable addition and illustrates how a difficult narrative ending could motivate scribes to provide resolution and further sayings. Principal limitation: Much of its content, including resurrection appearances and mission themes, has parallels elsewhere, so its removal need not erase the gospel message White is defending; its strongest force therefore concerns false textual attribution, whereas its force against resurrection belief or missionary teaching remains derivative. Live burden: Ehrman must keep textual addition distinct from doctrinal collapse, while White must explain why attributing added speech to Jesus is not already misquotation under the stated question. Locked score: The case is specific, causally explained, and directly concerns words placed on Jesus’ lips, making it excellent motion evidence even with modest doctrinal consequences, 89/100.

moves.words: White invokes Ehrman’s published agreement that textual variants generally do not affect essential Christian beliefs because disputed proof texts usually have support in other passages.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White uses a carefully delimited concession to distinguish local textual uncertainty from loss of central theology, directly challenging any slide from variant to religious unreliability. Principal limitation: The quotation addresses essential beliefs rather than whether a Bible can attribute nonoriginal words to Jesus, so it does not negate Ehrman’s literal motion criterion; the concession can establish redundancy of doctrinal support while leaving intact the historical accusation concerning words printed as Jesus’ own. Live burden: White must defend message continuity as the relevant meaning of “misquote,” while Ehrman must show that his affirmative remains important without exaggerating its theological reach. Locked score: The move is authoritative within the exchanged material and substantially narrows the affirmative’s implications, but it answers a stronger doctrinal thesis than the exact question requires, 89/100.

moves.words: Ehrman cites Jesus’ forgiveness prayer and Matthew’s statement that even the Son lacks end-time knowledge as sayings whose inclusion varies across early manuscript witnesses.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman moves beyond large acknowledged additions to compact sayings where a textual decision directly determines whether a particular claim is attributed to Jesus. Principal limitation: He presents the alternatives and continuing dispute but does not fully establish, within the debate, which reading is original in either example; their evidential posture establishes unresolved attribution more securely than it establishes the affirmative historical claim that either disputed wording was certainly secondary. Live burden: Ehrman needs only enough uncertainty or secondary attribution to sustain his historical-Bible claim, while White must show that recoverability or parallel teaching defeats the language of misquotation. Locked score: These examples are tightly aligned with the motion and show interpretive stakes, though unresolved originality restrains the certainty of the affirmative conclusion, 84/100.

moves.words: Ehrman presses White to identify the asserted dozen manuscripts within a century, disputes offered dates, and notes that citing authorities does not supply the missing list.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman subjects a rhetorically impressive numerical claim to direct audit and exposes that White cannot provide the complete dozen or defend each dating during the exchange. Principal limitation: Demonstrating incomplete substantiation in real time does not prove that the count is false, especially where manuscript dates remain ranges contested through cited scholarship; paleographical ranges and competing scholarly datings make courtroom-style demand for immediate enumeration probative of presentation quality, not conclusive of historical absence. Live burden: White must provide transparent membership and dating grounds for the early set; Ehrman must show how any corrected count changes the inference from dispersed attestation. Locked score: The cross-examination effectively lowers confidence in a central quantitative premise without overclaiming a disproof, and it appropriately distinguishes named authorities from accessible supporting evidence, 90/100.

moves.words: White argues that early witnesses from multiple intersecting transmission lines resist centralized alteration, since geographically dispersed copying preserves independent evidence rather than one controlled textual stream.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White replaces the telephone-chain picture with a branching transmission model and explains why uncontrolled geographical multiplication can preserve comparisons that reveal local changes. Principal limitation: His debated early-manuscript count is not fully itemized, and multiple later branches do not by themselves exclude a shared alteration before their divergence; the mechanism becomes decisive only if diversification predates the hypothesized shared corruption and the witnesses actually sample relevant independent ancestral pathways. Live burden: White must establish sufficiently early independence to bridge the autograph gap; Ehrman’s logically possible primitive bottleneck defeats a guarantee, while actual-corruption claims require evidence. Locked score: The distributed model is the negative’s most important structural answer and makes corruption harder to coordinate, but uncertainty about the earliest branch points limits its reach, 81/100.

moves.words: Ehrman accepts close agreement between P75 and Vaticanus within a proto-Alexandrian stream but asks what that relationship establishes about earlier copying nearer the original.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman isolates the inferential gap between demonstrating stable reproduction within one related stream and demonstrating accurate access to the autograph before that stream’s recoverable ancestor. Principal limitation: The challenge discounts neither Vaticanus readings older than P75 nor White’s broader appeal to intersecting lines beyond this particularly close pair; its focus on this celebrated comparison can also obscure the cumulative evidential force White claims from witnesses outside the proto-Alexandrian relationship. Live burden: White must show non-parent-child agreement is genealogically independent; only an affirmative claim of early corruption imposes a positive historical burden on Ehrman. Locked score: This precise genealogical objection blocks an easy leap from later agreement to original wording, though it remains a challenge to proof rather than positive evidence of corruption, 89/100.

moves.words: White argues that readings persist stubbornly once introduced, so the collective tradition contains original alternatives even alongside excess errors, making reconstruction a sorting problem.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White articulates why abundant variation can aid recovery: copying conserves even errors, leaving critics with surplus readings rather than an obviously depleted textual record. Principal limitation: Tenacity after a reading enters surviving transmission cannot guarantee preservation of autograph wording lost before the common ancestors represented by extant copies; the quoted scholarly confidence describes an impressive general transmission property, but White converts that tendency into an exceptionless conclusion requiring separate support. Live burden: White must justify observed persistence implying universal survival; Ehrman needs historical grounds only for an actual-lost-reading claim. Locked score: The premise gives preservation a coherent mechanism and explains the evidential value of abundance, but its strongest “none of the above” conclusion outruns what persistence alone demonstrates, 81/100.

moves.words: Ehrman answers tenacity by distinguishing possibility from probability and citing conjectural emendation, where critics judge that no surviving reading best explains the passage.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman directly attacks the modal overreach in White’s argument: an extant reading can possibly be original without making universal survival probable or evidentially secured. Principal limitation: His 1 Peter example is presented as a plausible scholarly conjecture, not a demonstrated instance in which the autograph reading certainly vanished; nor does professional willingness to propose emendation establish scholarly agreement that every extant option fails at the particular location he mentions. Live burden: Ehrman must supply passage-specific reasons for preferring an unattested reconstruction, while White must explain why tenacity warrants more than a practical presumption. Locked score: The response makes a decisive logical distinction and supplies a concrete critical practice that weakens categorical preservation, yet the illustrative emendation remains substantively contestable rather than a demonstrated lost reading, 90/100.

moves.words: White clarifies that P75 and Vaticanus share a broad stream without a direct parent-child relationship, with Vaticanus also preserving readings earlier than P75’s form.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White corrects an overly simple genealogy by distinguishing a textual stream from direct descent and uses divergent older readings in Vaticanus to argue for separate lines within that stream. Principal limitation: Independence from P75 is weaker than independence from every shared pre-P75 ancestor, so the clarification does not reach the autograph unaided; the terminology of separate lines within one stream risks sounding more independent than the evidence warrants unless their separation is established. Live burden: White must connect these partly independent witnesses to a sufficiently early and varied network; Ehrman must show why their agreement is compatible with his proposed bottleneck. Locked score: The answer materially improves the evidential picture and rebuts a direct-copy caricature, though it cannot alone establish that both lines bypassed every primitive alteration, 83/100.

moves.words: Ehrman proposes a Philippians countermodel where every surviving branch descends from an already mistaken third copy, allowing broad later agreement without autograph-level accuracy.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The hypothetical cleanly demonstrates that extensive branching, tenacity, and ninety-five-percent later agreement are logically compatible with shared errors introduced before the surviving family tree divides. Principal limitation: It is an underdetermination argument rather than historical evidence that Philippians or another book actually passed through such a single corrupted ancestor; without evidence about the initial copying history, the scenario equally permits faithful early exemplars and therefore primarily defeats necessity rather than supporting probability. Live burden: White must evidence diversification before consequential loss; Ehrman bears historical proof only if asserting an actual bottleneck. Locked score: As a counterexample to guaranteed recovery the move is rigorous and devastatingly clear, but its force stops short of proving any actual primitive corruption, 90/100.

moves.words: White argues that the emergence of recognizably the same New Testament books and theology across variant witnesses is improbable if major primitive corruption had displaced their original content.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White redirects attention from readings to the striking continuity of literary identity and theology across surviving witnesses, demanding an account of why alleged early corruption left one recognizable text. Principal limitation: One stable text can still contain local shared substitutions, additions, or omissions, which is enough for Ehrman’s narrower motion but not for wholesale textual replacement; recognizable literary and theological identity is compatible with bounded wording changes, interpolations, and inherited local errors conceded throughout the debate. Live burden: White must show that “same text” entails reliable individual quotation, while Ehrman must preserve the distinction between bounded local corruption and radical reconstruction. Locked score: The argument persuasively protects macro-level continuity and raises the cost of sweeping skepticism, but it cannot exclude the limited common-ancestor errors actually at issue, 82/100.

moves.words: Ehrman contrasts two readings in Mark 1:41—Jesus becoming angry or feeling compassion—to show that a local variant can materially change the scene’s portrayal.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman identifies a direct semantic contrast within the same narrated encounter: anger and compassion attribute materially different emotional responses to Jesus, so the variant is neither spelling nor stylistic noise. Principal limitation: Demonstrating a consequential difference between the alternatives does not demonstrate which reading is original, and this short exchange supplies no independent manuscript or transcriptional basis for choosing anger. Live burden: Ehrman must later justify originality before the contrast proves that a Bible misquotes Jesus; White must address the local portrayal rather than answer only with unchanged doctrine elsewhere. Locked score: The move establishes clear interpretive significance and keeps the dispute at an appropriately local scale, but its affirmative force remains conditional on the subsequent textual case, 87/100.

moves.words: White asks how “apart from God” can transform Hebrews if Ehrman also regards that reading as consistent with the letter’s theology and preferred internally.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White identifies an apparent tension between claiming book-level significance and defending a reading through consistency with Hebrews, forcing Ehrman to specify exactly what changes. Principal limitation: The challenge proportionately limits claims about transforming the whole book but does not decide which reading is original; thematic consistency elsewhere cannot eliminate the distinct comparative question of what Hebrews 2:9 explicitly states through comparative manuscript analysis. Live burden: White must separate thematic compatibility from explicit textual assertion, while Ehrman must state the alteration’s bounded interpretive consequence without implying an entirely different atonement. Locked score: The challenge usefully disciplines expansive rhetoric and elicits a sharper distinction, while leaving the external and internal evidence for the two readings unresolved, 89/100.

moves.words: Ehrman clarifies that Hebrews 2:9 uniquely states either death apart from God or death by God’s grace, changing the passage’s explicit account despite broader thematic consistency.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman answers at the correct level of granularity, distinguishing a theme compatible with Hebrews from the only explicit statement that Jesus died by divine grace. Principal limitation: The exchange does not independently settle which reading is original, and “apart from God” rests on limited manuscript evidence described by White; the claimed uniqueness heightens local importance, but uniqueness also makes external and patristic evidence especially necessary before preferring the more difficult formulation. Live burden: Ehrman must defend the preferred reading through internal and patristic support; White must show why uncertainty over this unique formulation is insignificant to the motion. Locked score: The clarification preserves a genuine semantic contrast without claiming wholesale doctrinal reversal, making it a strong example of how one variant changes an author’s express teaching, 87/100.

moves.words: White counters Mark’s anger reading with its thin support in a free witness, scholarly suspicion toward unsupported Bezae readings, and a plausible scribal harmonization from nearby forceful language.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White combines external evidence about the reading’s narrow attestation with a concrete internal mechanism by which an unusually expansive scribe could have introduced anger. Principal limitation: General distrust of Codex Bezae cannot decide this location, and the proposed harmonization competes with Ehrman’s equally specific easier-reading account; because both proposed scribal motives are psychologically plausible, general manuscript character cannot replace detailed evaluation of wording, sequence, and comparative transcriptional habits. Live burden: White must show his local transcriptional story better predicts the evidence; Ehrman must explain why a poorly supported difficult reading survives only in this witness. Locked score: The rebuttal directly engages both manuscript quality and scribal motive, creating a balanced textual contest rather than relying on raw witness counting, 88/100.

moves.words: Ehrman separates Bezae’s general unreliability from this reading’s internal merits and limits the consequence to a fuller nuance in Mark’s recurring depiction of Jesus’ anger.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman refuses a blanket witness judgment and accurately narrows his conclusion: the variant enriches a recurring Markan characterization rather than producing an entirely different book. Principal limitation: Markan internal coherence and a plausible softening motive do not resolve the adverse external evidence; his interpretation must still explain why the anger reading has thin support in a notably free witness while compassion dominates the geographically broader tradition. Live burden: Ehrman must compare directional scribal probabilities without overvaluing thematic fit; White must show why his addition theory better explains the specific wording. Locked score: The measured qualification strengthens credibility and preserves meaningful local interpretation, while the underlying textual choice remains too contested to bear a sweeping conclusion, 89/100.

moves.words: Ehrman challenges White’s ninety-five-percent figure by distinguishing representative printed editions from individual manuscripts and asking how actual Byzantine-Alexandrian manuscript word agreement would compare.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman exposes that a percentage depends on what is compared and counted, separating editorial platforms, total words, and variant-unit family assignments. Principal limitation: White had expressly labeled the comparison as printed texts, and the lack of a manuscript collation does not invalidate the reproducible claim actually made about those editions; at moments the questioning presses a manuscript-pair statistic that White never claimed to possess, so exposure of scope does not amount to numerical refutation. Live burden: Ehrman must establish why printed endpoints misrepresent historical witness diversity; White must prevent audiences from transferring edition-level agreement to manuscript-level uniformity. Locked score: The move provides the debate’s sharpest denominator audit and blocks an easy statistical inference, though it sometimes presses White for a different calculation than the one presented, 91/100.

moves.words: White defends his computer comparison as a disclosed test between printed Byzantine and Westcott-Hort endpoints, yielding roughly ninety-five-percent agreement across total words rather than variant units.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White consistently states the objects and denominator of his calculation and offers a reproducible procedure instead of disguising printed editions as manuscript collations. Principal limitation: Editorial endpoint texts compress variation within manuscript families, so their agreement cannot directly quantify pairwise agreement among historical copies or prove autograph recovery; a reader could reasonably mistake editorial convergence at selected endpoints for direct measurement of historical-copy agreement unless that inferential boundary remains prominent. Live burden: White must explain what inference the edition comparison legitimately supports; Ehrman must show that its abstraction materially biases the perceived stability. Locked score: The statistic is transparent and useful for illustrating broad textual overlap, but its evidential scope is narrower than the audience-facing manuscript-stability impression it encourages, 86/100.

moves.words: Ehrman rejects percentage alone as a measure of importance, observing that changing a single negation in one hundred words can reverse a sentence’s meaning.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The negation example decisively shows that edit distance and semantic consequence are different variables, preventing high verbal agreement from mechanically settling interpretive reliability. Principal limitation: It is a generic illustration and does not show that surviving New Testament variants regularly, or even in the cited cases, reverse entire propositions in that manner; the example establishes measurement principle, not empirical frequency, and therefore needs the Hebrews, Mark, and sayings disputes to supply its actual textual relevance. Live burden: Ehrman must connect low-frequency differences to actual consequential examples; White must evaluate significance case by case rather than infer it from percentage. Locked score: The conceptual correction is simple, rigorous, and indispensable to interpreting White’s figures, though its hypothetical severity cannot substitute for passage-specific evidence, 90/100.

moves.words: White argues that applying Ehrman’s uncertainty standard consistently would destabilize quotation of far more sparsely attested classical authors, despite historians routinely using their transmitted texts.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White tests consistency through a relevant comparison and emphasizes that historical knowledge ordinarily operates without autographs or absolute certainty, placing New Testament transmission within broader ancient practice. Principal limitation: Ehrman accepts the same textual uncertainty for classical works while still permitting qualified historical use, so the challenge targets total skepticism he does not endorse; relative manuscript abundance can increase confidence without erasing Ehrman’s accepted point that specific readings in every ancient tradition remain probabilistic and revisable. Live burden: White must show that Ehrman’s actual limited claim has untenable consequences; Ehrman must make his qualifications explicit whenever he quotes reconstructed ancient texts. Locked score: The analogy effectively rebuts an impossible-certainty requirement, but its force diminishes once Ehrman grants fallible quotation across all ancient literature, 81/100.

moves.words: Ehrman accepts that classical texts share the autograph problem and explains that scholars quote their best manuscript traditions while openly retaining uncertainty about some original words.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman answers the consistency test without special pleading, applying one fallibilist standard to Suetonius, Tacitus, Plato, Thomas, and the New Testament alike. Principal limitation: Applying the same uncertainty consistently establishes methodological parity, but it does not quantify uncertainty for any cited author or determine the reliability of a particular passage; his qualified position concerns disputed wording rather than equal doubt across every line of each work. Live burden: Ehrman must distinguish local uncertainty from global unknowability; White must engage that bounded position rather than equate it with abandonment of history. Locked score: The answer preserves ordinary historical reasoning while conceding its textual limits, decisively neutralizing the alleged double standard and avoiding the radical skepticism attributed to him, 92/100.

moves.words: White presses that Ehrman nevertheless quotes classical writers as usable sources, suggesting that sufficient textual knowledge survives even when manuscripts are late and comparatively scarce.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White extracts an important practical concession: lack of originals and residual uncertainty do not prevent responsible quotation, interpretation, or historical argument from transmitted texts. Principal limitation: Usability is compatible with occasional misquotation in surviving copies, so the concession supports broad reliability more clearly than it defeats the exact motion; qualified citation shows practical confidence but does not entail that every transmitted sentence, attribution, or exact word survives without recoverable or irrecoverable alteration. Live burden: White must define a recoverability threshold relevant to attributing Jesus’ words; Ehrman must avoid presenting uncertainty as uniform across every passage. Locked score: The follow-up grounds abstract standards in scholarly conduct and strengthens the case for a usable New Testament, yet it leaves local disputed wording substantially untouched, 85/100.

moves.words: Ehrman explains that his expectation of divinely inspired words being perfectly preserved is a personal theological judgment motivating his interest, not the central textual argument of his book.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman explicitly labels the preservation expectation personal and subsidiary, preventing it from masquerading as a historical inference while candidly explaining why textual instability mattered to his former belief. Principal limitation: He repeatedly defends the intuition that inspiration should entail preservation, despite offering no independent premise about what a deity would choose to do; that intuition also addresses the compatibility of inspiration and transmission history, a theological problem separable from whether a surviving copy misattributes speech. Live burden: Ehrman must keep the theological expectation separate from evidence for misquotation; White must answer it without treating its failure as a refutation of Ehrman’s textual cases. Locked score: The disclosure is honest and relevant, but as argument it relies on a contestable divine-intention premise outside the motion’s strongest evidential path, 77/100.

moves.words: White argues that apostles freely used Old Testament translations without originals, showing that inspiration historically did not require perfectly identical copies or direct autograph access.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White supplies an internal theological counterexample to Ehrman’s preservation expectation: authoritative apostolic practice operated through translated, textually varied forms rather than an exact-copy standard. Principal limitation: The argument rebuts a requirement of perfect preservation but does not establish that every attribution within those copies is original or answer specific variants; translation practice may authorize semantic fidelity across wording differences, but it does not automatically authenticate additions lacking a source counterpart. Live burden: White must connect apostolic functional use to the debate’s ordinary meaning of quotation; Ehrman must explain why his personal standard should govern inspiration after conceding it was not theirs. Locked score: The move strongly defeats the claimed theological entailment and uses evidence accepted within the discussion, while leaving the historical misquotation question partly independent, 89/100.

moves.words: Ehrman concedes that perfect preservation was not the apostles’ standard, then notes their quotations sometimes reflect Old Testament textual forms unavailable in present Bibles.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman forthrightly yields the historical-theological point instead of evading it and redirects attention to the continuing reality that scriptural quotation itself occurs through differing textual forms. Principal limitation: His observation about Matthew is asserted briefly and does not demonstrate whether the unavailable form reflects textual loss, interpretive adaptation, or another source; the response consequently complicates exact-copy expectations more than it vindicates Ehrman’s earlier inference from imperfect preservation to doubtful original inspiration. Live burden: Ehrman must abandon any claim that apostolic practice supports his personal preservation criterion; White must still account for how variant forms affect exact attribution. Locked score: The concession accurately narrows the dispute and preserves a relevant textual complication, making the exchange productive even though the supporting Old Testament example remains underdeveloped, 90/100.

moves.words: White argues that Christian education about textual criticism prevents shock, while uncontrolled Mediterranean expansion kept any authority from centrally altering the New Testament’s message.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White joins a practical recommendation to a historical mechanism: informed readers can acknowledge famous additions without panic because dispersed copying denied any editor control over the entire tradition. Principal limitation: Decentralization blocks coordinated later revision more readily than it excludes local or primitive alterations inherited before wide dispersion, and education itself proves no reading; its pastoral warning concerns responsible reception and cannot independently determine the genealogy or originality of any contested wording attributed to Jesus. Live burden: White must date meaningful diversification early enough to support preservation; Ehrman must explain why admitted additions matter without exploiting uninformed expectations. Locked score: The move responsibly normalizes textual criticism and reinforces message continuity, though its confident preservation narrative still depends on the contested earliest transmission period, 82/100.

moves.words: Ehrman defines the motion historically: most Christians possessed particular manuscript Bibles, all with mistakes, including changes within words attributed to Jesus, rather than modern reconstructed editions.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman makes the debate’s object explicit and ties his conclusion to actual Bibles used across history, where individual manuscripts indisputably differed at passages reporting Jesus’ speech. Principal limitation: “All Bibles” is rhetorically overbroad unless misquotation includes any copying error within Jesus material, regardless of whether the specific intended quotation remains recoverable elsewhere; the universal quantifier holds only under a broad definition counting any local scribal difference within reported speech as a misquotation by that copy. Live burden: Ehrman must defend that ordinary-language criterion; White must explain why recoverability across witnesses prevents a mistaken historical copy from misquoting. Locked score: This closing synthesis directly answers the wording of the motion and exploits the gap between collective reconstruction and any particular manuscript, although its universal phrasing requires careful qualification, 87/100.

moves.words: White closes that variants are not misquotations because the collective evidence preserves what Jesus and the apostles taught, without altering the recognizable gospel or essential theology.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: White offers a coherent final standard centered on recoverable teaching and message continuity, integrating manuscript abundance, tenacity, dispersed transmission, and acknowledged doctrinal stability. Principal limitation: His consistently broader message standard does not directly answer the ordinary case where a historical Bible assigns a secondary sentence or wording to Jesus; recoverable theology and recognizable books answer whether Christianity’s central proclamation survived, not whether every reported sentence in every Bible originated with Jesus. Live burden: White must show why collective recoverability governs the noun “Bible” in the question; Ehrman must avoid inflating local errors into global unreliability. Locked score: The synthesis robustly defeats sweeping claims of theological corruption and historical collapse, but it does not fully negate the narrower literal proposition Ehrman established, 85/100.

strengths: Ehrman anchors the motion in concrete, substantial passages and disputed sayings, showing how historical copies could place secondary wording or entire episodes on Jesus’ lips.

His bottleneck model exposes a real logical gap between later branching and guaranteed autograph recovery, while his denominator critique prevents printed-edition agreement from masquerading as manuscript uniformity.
He consistently distinguishes meaningful local uncertainty from total historical skepticism and ultimately limits Mark’s anger variant to nuance rather than claiming it rewrites the entire Gospel.

blunders.text: The opening copying-chain picture is too linear and initially underrepresents the intersecting transmission lines that make comparison and correction possible.
His personal claim that inspiration should entail perfect preservation lacks an independently defended account of divine intentions and is weakened by his concession about apostolic practice.

strengths: White supplies the debate’s essential taxonomy, separating raw variant totals from viable, meaningful readings and preventing trivial scribal differences from carrying exaggerated argumentative weight.

His distributed-transmission and tenacity arguments explain how uncontrolled manuscript abundance can preserve alternatives, expose changes, and sustain broad continuity without requiring any flawless individual copy.

He effectively establishes that major additions do not create essential Christian beliefs and that ordinary historical reasoning can use ancient texts despite missing autographs and residual uncertainty.

blunders.text: The asserted dozen manuscripts within a century remains incompletely listed and defended when challenged, weakening a conspicuous quantitative premise about exceptionally early attestation.
His closing standard emphasizes stable message and theology so heavily that it does not squarely answer whether particular historical Bibles sometimes attribute nonoriginal wording to Jesus.

finalArgument.thesis: A Bible misquotes Jesus when its received text attributes wording to him that was not in the earliest recoverable form.
premises: Historical Christians ordinarily encountered particular manuscript Bibles rather than a modern apparatus combining evidence from the whole surviving tradition.
Some manuscript forms include extended episodes or sayings attributed to Jesus that both debaters accept or allow are textually secondary.
Collective recoverability can help modern critics identify an addition without making the earlier manuscript that contained it an accurate quotation.
Stable theology elsewhere does not convert a locally secondary saying into Jesus’ original words within the copy that reports it.
Therefore message continuity and local misquotation can both be true without implying that the entire New Testament is historically unusable.
finalArgument.conclusion: Because at least some historically used Bibles assigned secondary wording to Jesus, the motion is affirmed even though the broader apostolic message remains substantially recoverable.

newArguments.title: Redundancy Is Not Authentication
newArguments.text: White’s doctrinal redundancy answer has an unexpected implication. When a disputed saying has theological support elsewhere, that protects the belief while conceding that this particular textual attribution can be evaluated independently. Parallel support cannot authenticate the contested words; it only reduces the cost of removing them. Thus the stronger White makes redundancy, the easier it becomes to affirm local misquotation without inferring doctrinal collapse.

newArguments.title: Correction Confirms Earlier Error
newArguments.text: Modern brackets and textual notes do more than display uncertainty: they are corrective responses to earlier received forms that presented disputed material without those qualifications. Successful correction therefore has a temporal implication. It can improve a current Bible while confirming that prior Bibles made an unqualified attribution requiring repair. Recovery evidence answers what later editors can know, but the act of repair remains evidence about what earlier readers were told.

finalArgument.thesis: Textual variation does not amount to biblical misquotation when the collective manuscript record preserves recoverable teaching and transparent alternatives.
premises: A large, geographically dispersed manuscript tradition naturally produces more recorded differences while also supplying more evidence for comparison and correction.
Most documented variants are nonmeaningful, nonviable, or recognizable scribal errors rather than credible competing reports of Jesus’ teaching.
Even famous secondary passages can be identified through the tradition and do not uniquely sustain the essential theology attributed to Jesus and the apostles.
Historical quotation never requires possession of an autograph or absolute certainty at every word, as ordinary use of classical sources demonstrates.
Calling every variant a misquotation obscures the difference between a flawed individual copy and the recoverable textual tradition represented by the Bible.
finalArgument.conclusion: Since the tradition exposes its own copying differences while preserving recognizable teaching and usable wording, textual variants alone do not justify saying that the Bible misquotes Jesus.

newArguments.title: Corrective Transparency
newArguments.text: A tradition that openly preserves rival readings differs epistemically from a single corrupted report whose error cannot be detected. Brackets, footnotes, and comparative witnesses make disputed attributions visible and revisable. If “the Bible” denotes the critically presented textual tradition rather than every historical copy, its disclosure of uncertainty can prevent a false assertion rather than constitute one. The negative should therefore ground its case in transparent recoverability, not perfection.

newArguments.title: Distributed Error Correction
newArguments.text: The manuscript tradition can be modeled as redundant transmission rather than a contest among individually perfect copies. When independent branches preserve overlapping content and different local mistakes, agreement identifies stable material while disagreement marks locations needing review. This inference does not guarantee that every original reading survives, but it makes recoverability a property of the network rather than any manuscript. White’s case is strongest when framed as probabilistic error correction with acknowledged residual uncertainty.

noveltyMap.title: Redundancy Is Not Authentication
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Shows that parallel doctrinal support protects a belief without authenticating the disputed attribution, so White’s redundancy defense can reduce consequences while leaving the local affirmative claim intact.

noveltyMap.title: Correction Confirms Earlier Error
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Derives a temporal inference from modern correction: brackets and notes can improve present editions while evidencing that earlier unqualified received forms required repair.

noveltyMap.title: Corrective Transparency
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Argues that preserving and disclosing competing readings changes the epistemic character of the Bible as a critical tradition, potentially preventing rather than asserting a false quotation.

noveltyMap.title: Distributed Error Correction
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Models recoverability as a probabilistic network property produced by overlapping independent branches and differently located errors, without assuming perfection or guaranteed universal survival.

editorialReview.sourceFidelity: Every card names the passage, manuscript relationship, numerical comparison, or theological inference actually argued in this debate; excluded audience material supplies no assessment credit.
editorialReview.completeQuotes: Both featured quotations reproduce exact canonical-caption wording as complete standalone thoughts, with contexts that preserve historical scope, speaker purpose, and necessary qualifications.
editorialReview.scoreConsistency: All thirty-two locked move scores and the controlling 88–86 pro result remain unchanged; no prose adjustment covertly revises assessment substance or weighting.
editorialReview.nonformulaicCritiques: Beyond the four mandatory sentence labels, each critique uses move-specific evidence, identifies a distinct inferential weakness, and frames burdens tailored to that precise exchange.
editorialReview.aiContributionNonformulaic: The four new arguments contribute distinct inferences about doctrinal redundancy, temporal correction, disclosure, and network-level error correction rather than repackaging the speakers’ live claims.
editorialReview.aiPunctuation: All final-argument premises, conclusions, new arguments, critiques, contexts, strengths, blunders, novelty explanations, and editorial attestations end with appropriate terminal punctuation.
editorialReview.referenceComparison: Independent reference profiles informed quality control only; the candidate follows the frozen debate evidence, preserves disagreements, and imports no outside historical adjudication.
